intro.t: The same history, retold for the returned exiles.
b: Chronicles covers much of Samuel and Kings again, but written after the exile for people rebuilding. The genealogies that open it establish continuity for a community that felt cut off from its past.
The emphasis falls on the temple, worship, and the Davidic line — the things that gave a diminished community its identity.

17.t: Chronicles retells 2 Samuel 7 for the returned exiles, for whom the promise to David was the reason to hope at all.
David's response to the covenant is to sit down and ask why. Neither triumph nor false modesty.

29.t: Everything comes from your hand, and of your own we have given you. The theology of giving in two sentences.

29.h: Who am I, and who are my people
29.t: Everything comes from your hand and we have given you only what comes from your hand. Said while giving on an enormous scale.

21.t: David counts his fighting men and is judged for it. He refuses to offer a sacrifice that costs him nothing.

28.h: Know the God of your father
28.t: And serve him with wholehearted devotion, for the LORD searches every heart. David's charge to Solomon.

1.t: Chronicles opens with genealogies from Adam onward, written for returned exiles who needed to know they were still the same people.

10.t: Chronicles gives the theological summary Samuel leaves implicit: he was unfaithful and did not enquire of the LORD.

11.t: Three men break through enemy lines for a drink and David pours it out rather than drink it. Loyalty honoured by refusing to consume it.

16.t: A psalm assembled from parts of Psalms 105, 96 and 106, sung when the ark came to Jerusalem.

22.t: David is told he will not build the temple. He spends the rest of his life collecting materials for the son who will.

4.t: Two verses inside nine chapters of names. It became a bestseller in 2000; in context it is one man among hundreds.

13.t: The ark moved on a new cart rather than carried by Levites, as chapter 15 later acknowledges.

15.t: David says no one but the Levites may carry the ark, because we did not enquire how to do it in the prescribed way.

23.t: Detailed rotas for worship. Chronicles cares about this because its readers were rebuilding exactly this.

2.t: The genealogy slows down as it reaches David. The writer is heading for the king.

3.t: Traced past the exile. The line survived.

5.t: A tribal war won because they trusted him, noted in the middle of a genealogy.

6.t: Heman, Asaph and Ethan, whose names head many psalms.

7.t: Recorded even though the north had been destroyed. The writer insists all twelve belong.

8.t: The genealogy of the first king, preserved alongside David's.

9.t: The first to return are listed. The genealogies were written for exactly these people.

12.t: The men of Issachar knew what Israel should do. A phrase often borrowed, and rightly.

14.t: Twice, and receives different instructions each time. Past guidance does not replace present asking.

18.t: David's reign summarised, as in 2 Samuel 8.

19.t: Retold without the Bathsheba episode, which Chronicles omits. The Chronicler is writing to encourage, not to record everything.

20.t: The Chronicler skips straight from the siege to its end.

24.t: Twenty-four courses. Zechariah, John the Baptist's father, served in the course of Abijah.

25.t: Music in worship is described as a form of prophecy. Worship leaders were appointed by lot, young and old alike.

26.t: Even the doorkeepers are named. Chronicles honours ordinary service.

27.t: Twelve units, each serving one month. Administration recorded as part of faithful kingship.
